::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Congenital syphilis (CS) remains one of the most preventable yet persistent infectious causes of perinatal morbidity and mortality worldwide.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated 661,000 cases of CS in 2016, resulting in 355,000 adverse birth outcomes, including stillbirths, neonatal deaths, preterm births and low birth weight [1].
text.formatted: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated 661,000 cases of CS in 2016, resulting in 355,000 adverse birth outcomes, including stillbirths, neonatal deaths, preterm births and low birth weight <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: The burden of syphilis among women of reproductive age remains substantial [2], and the WHO validation criteria for elimination of mother-to-child transmission require a CS incidence of 50 or fewer cases per 100,000 live births, together with antenatal screening and treatment coverage of at least 95% [3].

text.text: In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 29,149 CS cases in 2020, 76% of them in Brazil [4].

text.text: In Colombia, the prevalence ratio of gestational syphilis doubled between 2019 and 2024, from 11.1 to 22.0 per 1,000 live births plus fetal deaths, and 1,097 CS cases were notified in 2024, an incidence of 2.5 per 1,000 live births plus fetal deaths, five times the elimination threshold [5].

text.text: Among these cases, 90.4% of maternal diagnoses occurred in the third trimester, 37.4% of mothers had no prenatal care and only half received at least one dose of treatment [5].

text.text: These figures indicate a systemic failure of early prenatal serological screening, a paradox given that benzathine penicillin prevents vertical transmission when administered appropriately and at least 30 days before delivery [6].

text.text: National clinical practice guidelines therefore recommend syphilis screening at the first prenatal visit, with repeat testing in each trimester and at delivery [7].

text.text: The biological basis for this window is well established: the ability of Treponema pallidum subsp. pallidum to cross the placental barrier increases from approximately 16 weeks of gestation onward, making early detection the critical intervention point [8].

text.text: CS is also re-emerging in high-income settings.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reported 78 confirmed CS cases across the European Union and European Economic Area in 2023, with increases that paralleled rising syphilis notification rates among women [9].

text.text: David et al. framed CS in Switzerland as a marker of inequality, because cases concentrated where prenatal screening, treatment continuity and access to care failed [10].

text.text: These findings support the interpretation of CS as a sentinel event for inequities in access to timely prenatal and sexually transmitted infection care.

The Subred Integrada de Servicios de Salud Sur E.S.E. (Subred Sur) is a public health service network in southern Bogotá that integrates primary care units and referral hospitals serving the localities of Ciudad Bolívar, Usme, Tunjuelito and Sumapaz, among the lowest-income areas of the city, and attends approximately 6,000 deliveries annually [11].

text.text: We aimed to identify maternal and prenatal care factors independently associated with CS over an 8-year period in this large, socially complex urban public health network.
We conducted a retrospective case-control study using routinely collected data from January 1, 2017, through December 31, 2024.
The study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines [21] (S1 Checklist).
text.formatted: The study is reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> (S1 Checklist).

text.text: The Subred Sur is the sole public integrated health network in southern Bogotá, serving a population of approximately 1.3 million inhabitants; it provides obstetric care regardless of insurance status and is the primary referral network for migrants and other vulnerable populations.

Data were obtained from the institutional communicable disease databases of the Early Warning team of the Subred Sur Health Risk Management Directorate, institutional electronic health records, cases notified to the Colombian national public health surveillance system (SIVIGILA) and the national birth and death registry (RUAF).

All women with gestational syphilis confirmed according to the criteria of the Colombian National Institute of Health (INS) whose pregnancy ended at a Subred Sur facility during the study period were eligible.
Pregnancies ending in out-of-facility delivery, spontaneous abortion, ectopic pregnancy or induced abortion were excluded.

Cases were neonates diagnosed with CS according to INS national surveillance criteria [22], which are consistent with WHO definitions and complementary to the diagnostic standards of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [23]: a case is confirmed when either an epidemiological criterion (neonate born to a mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis) or a laboratory criterion (neonatal nontreponemal antibody titer at least fourfold higher than the maternal titer at delivery) is met.
text.formatted: Cases were neonates diagnosed with CS according to INS national surveillance criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, which are consistent with WHO definitions and complementary to the diagnostic standards of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>: a case is confirmed when either an epidemiological criterion (neonate born to a mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis) or a laboratory criterion (neonatal nontreponemal antibody titer at least fourfold higher than the maternal titer at delivery) is met.

text.text: Controls were neonates without CS born to mothers with confirmed gestational syphilis who delivered within the same network during the same period.
All eligible controls identified over the eight-year study period were included, without sampling or matching, yielding an observed case-to-control ratio of 1:1.6.
Because controls were not selected through matching, unconditional logistic regression was used for all analyses.
Under the INS surveillance definition, a neonate born to a mother with untreated or inadequately treated syphilis is classified as a case on epidemiological grounds alone.

Maternal treatment adequacy (completion of benzathine penicillin at least 30 days before delivery) is therefore a component of the outcome definition rather than an independent exposure, and, by construction, all control mothers had received adequate treatment.
For this reason, maternal treatment was not analysed as a risk factor; it is reported descriptively to characterise the care pathway, and no measure of association is presented for it.
Gestational age at diagnosis is also related to the case definition, because diagnosis late in pregnancy shortens the interval available to complete treatment 30 days before delivery.
It does not, however, determine case status: women diagnosed after 28 weeks may still complete treatment within this window before a term delivery, as occurred in 15.7% of controls.
Late diagnosis was therefore retained as an exposure, and its estimate is interpreted in light of this structural relationship (see Limitations).
Sample size was determined by the total number of eligible records over the study period (census sampling).

To assess whether this sample was sufficient, we estimated the minimum size required to detect an odds ratio of 2.0 with a two-sided α of 0.05, 80% power and a 1:2 case-tocontrol ratio, assuming an exposure prevalence of 16% among controls (Kelsey method) [24]; the required sample was 158 cases and 315 controls.

text.text: Because the exposure prevalence was derived from the study controls, this calculation is post hoc and is reported only to show that the available sample exceeded the minimum requirement.

The unit of analysis was the pregnant woman, because the exposures of interest (timeliness of diagnosis, treatment and access to prenatal care) are measured in the mother, although the outcome occurs in the neonate.

Four variables were not entered into the multivariable model.

Adequate benzathine penicillin treatment was not entered into the regression models because it is a component of the case definition; the complete separation observed (all 458 controls vs. 4 of 285 cases [1.4%]) is a direct consequence of this definitional overlap rather than an empirical finding.

Partner treatment adequacy showed a bivariate association (crude OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.11-2.02; p = 0.009) but was not retained after backward elimination because it did not meet the retention criterion (p < 0.10) after adjustment for the remaining covariates; this likely reflects collinearity with reinfection, as both capture failure of the partner management pathway.

text.text: Lack of health insurance was excluded as an upstream structural determinant acting through access to prenatal care, because its inclusion risked overadjustment for a mediator.
Preterm delivery was excluded a priori on causal grounds, because T. pallidum infection can induce preterm labour, making temporal sequencing indeterminate in retrospective data.
Categorical variables were described as frequencies and proportions and non-normally distributed continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs).

Crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated by simple logistic regression, and group differences were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test or the Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate.

Variables with a bivariate p < 0.20 and less than 10% missing data were candidates for multivariable analysis; this inclusive threshold was chosen to avoid the premature exclusion of variables that may act as confounders once other covariates are considered [26].

279 Discussion 280 The factors identified in this 8-year case-control study suggest that CS in a socially complex 281 urban setting is associated primarily with failures in timely diagnosis and sustained access to 282 prenatal care, rather than with limitations of the available therapeutic tools.
Late maternal diagnosis after 28 weeks of gestation showed the strongest association with CS (aOR 17.75).

This finding is consistent with a cohort from Suzhou, China, in which diagnosis after 36 weeks was associated with markedly higher CS risk than first-trimester diagnosis [16], and with multicentre data from Switzerland, where diagnosis in the second or third trimester was strongly associated with a late first antenatal visit [17].
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with a cohort from Suzhou, China, in which diagnosis after 36 weeks was associated with markedly higher CS risk than first-trimester diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, and with multicentre data from Switzerland, where diagnosis in the second or third trimester was strongly associated with a late first antenatal visit <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Although gestational thresholds differed across studies, the direction of association consistently shows that delayed diagnosis sharply reduces the opportunity for effective prevention before delivery.
Part of the magnitude observed here, however, reflects the structural link between late diagnosis and the case definition described in the Methods.
In Colombia, 90.4% of maternal diagnoses among CS cases occur in the third trimester [5], situating the Subred Sur findings within a broader national failure of early prenatal screening.

text.text: Absence of prenatal care was associated with nearly 13-fold higher odds of CS.

In a systematic review of 14 studies, Pascoal et al. identified inadequate or late prenatal care and inadequate or late maternal treatment as significant risk factors for CS [14], and Etti et al. reported absent prenatal care, late diagnosis and incomplete treatment as the main determinants of vertical transmission in Fortaleza, Brazil [15].

text.text: The higher magnitude observed here likely reflects the extreme social vulnerability of the catchment population.

Low prenatal care utilisation cannot be explained solely by supply-side barriers: structural and psychosocial factors, including fear of a sexually transmitted infection diagnosis, intimate partner coercion, substance use and institutional distrust, act as barriers that expanding service coverage alone cannot overcome [25].

text.text: These findings underscore the need for systematic, active partner management and contact tracing.
Prior syphilis history was associated with 55% lower odds of CS (aOR 0.45).

This likely reflects differential clinical pathways: previously identified women enter subsequent pregnancies already flagged in the health record, enabling earlier serological screening and diagnosis at earlier gestational stages.
Pascoal et al. likewise identified a prior history of adequately treated syphilis as a protective factor [14].

text.text: Systematic documentation of sexually transmitted infection history and differentiated monitoring protocols for women with prior syphilis are low-cost interventions that warrant evaluation [22].

text.text: Only 4 of 285 case mothers (1.4%) had documented adequate treatment before delivery.
Because treatment adequacy is part of the surveillance case definition, this proportion describes the care pathway of cases rather than providing an independent estimate of treatment effect.

Its relevance lies in what preceded it: the conditions that precluded timely treatment, namely late diagnosis and absent prenatal care, were the factors most strongly associated with CS in this population, which is consistent with the high efficacy of benzathine penicillin when administered at least 30 days before delivery [6, 23].

text.text: Under the INS definition, the four adequately treated case mothers would have been classified through the laboratory criterion, and may represent treatment failure or reinfection close to delivery.

Insurance status showed a crude association (OR 2.05) but was excluded from the model as an upstream determinant of access to prenatal care; in this institutional context, it also reflects differential ascertainment between public and contributoryregime networks.
Preterm delivery (20.7% of cases vs.

5.7% of controls) was not modelled as a risk factor, because T. pallidum infection can cause placental inflammation, fetal growth restriction and preterm labour, so that preterm birth may represent a consequence of uncontrolled fetal infection rather than an antecedent exposure.
It is better interpreted as a clinical marker of the severity of untreated vertical transmission, as is the frequency of fetal death or stillbirth among cases (9.8% vs.
0.2% of controls).
Preterm birth is one of the main adverse birth outcomes attributed to untreated maternal syphilis worldwide [1].

text.text: Migrant status was associated with CS in the crude analysis, but the association was attenuated after adjustment, a pattern also described in China [16].

text.text: This suggests that migration does not directly increase the risk of vertical transmission but acts through conditions associated with social vulnerability and access barriers, such as late diagnosis and absent prenatal care.

Studies in Switzerland documented a high proportion of foreign-born mothers among CS cases [17], and in the United States public insurance has been associated with a higher frequency of syphilis during pregnancy, reflecting structural inequalities in prenatal access [31].
text.formatted: Studies in Switzerland documented a high proportion of foreign-born mothers among CS cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, and in the United States public insurance has been associated with a higher frequency of syphilis during pregnancy, reflecting structural inequalities in prenatal access <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: These findings collectively point to a single structural gap: the most vulnerable women access care late, intermittently or not at all.
Fragmented care across institutions also means that prior syphilis history, previous serological titres and partner treatment records are often unavailable at the point of care.

Universal first-trimester syphilis screening, with mandatory repeat testing in the third trimester for migrants, uninsured women and women without prior prenatal care, may be the most effective programmatic priority [6, 7, 23, 25].

text.text: Systematic partner management could be protocolised as a condition for case closure [13, 15], and interoperable obstetric records would enable differentiated follow-up of women with prior sexually transmitted infections, a low-cost intervention that warrants evaluation [22].
text.formatted: Systematic partner management could be protocolised as a condition for case closure <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>, and interoperable obstetric records would enable differentiated follow-up of women with prior sexually transmitted infections, a low-cost intervention that warrants evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: As a retrospective study, findings depend on the completeness of clinical records, which may be compromised when women received care at multiple institutions, potentially leading to underestimation of prenatal contacts and treatment episodes.
Several exposures are structurally related to the outcome definition.

The INS criterion prioritises surveillance sensitivity over diagnostic specificity and classifies neonates of untreated or inadequately treated mothers as cases, so some neonates classified on epidemiological linkage alone may represent probable rather than microbiologically confirmed CS.

For the same reason, maternal treatment adequacy could not be evaluated as a risk factor, and associations for variables that determine the opportunity to treat, particularly late diagnosis, are likely to be larger than they would be under a microbiological case definition.
This partial incorporation of exposure into the outcome may therefore inflate the magnitude, although not the direction, of the association observed for late diagnosis.
The distribution of cases by classification criterion was not available, which precluded a sensitivity analysis restricted to laboratory-confirmed cases.

In selected atypical cases, complementary molecular tools such as digital PCR and next-generation sequencing can support diagnostic confirmation, as recently shown in a CS case from the same institution [32].
text.formatted: In selected atypical cases, complementary molecular tools such as digital PCR and next-generation sequencing can support diagnostic confirmation, as recently shown in a CS case from the same institution <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Surveillance bias may affect reinfection detection, because women with more prenatal contacts have more opportunities for repeat serological testing, potentially leading to overestimation of reinfection prevalence in the better-monitored subgroup.
The adjusted model used complete-case analysis and excluded 25 participants with missing data.
Information on income, employment, intimate partner violence, social support and housing conditions was not available, and these factors may act as residual confounders.

Finally, results are specific to this public network and may not represent CS epidemiology across the whole city; however, the structural risk patterns identified, including the mediating role of migration through access barriers and the concentration of vulnerability in public networks, may inform prevention strategies in comparable urban settings with high migration pressure.

Late gestational syphilis diagnosis, absent prenatal care and reinfection were the factors most strongly associated with CS in this high-vulnerability urban public network over eight years, while a prior history of syphilis was independently associated with lower odds of CS.
CS persistence reflects systemic failures in diagnostic timeliness and continuity of prenatal care rather than the absence of effective therapeutic tools.

Strategies likely to reduce CS in socially vulnerable urban populations include early capture of pregnant women, universal first-trimester syphilis screening with third-trimester repetition, timely benzathine penicillin treatment and comprehensive management of sexual partners.
